lessons.title: Why seed samples are stored
lessons.html:
Why seed samples are stored

After a seed laboratory has tested a sample, the unused part, and sometimes separate reference samples, must be kept. These stored samples are evidence. If a farmer complains about poor emergence, or an inspector questions a label, the laboratory can retest the stored sample of that exact lot. Without it, nobody can prove what quality the seed had when it was sold.

Kinds of stored samples

  • Retained (reference) samples of each seed lot that was tested and labelled.
  • Remnants of submitted samples after testing.
  • Components from purity analysis, such as prohibited weed seeds found.
  • Samples on hold because of a complaint or dispute.

Each kind may have a different storage period. The laboratory procedure and the seed regulations that apply set how long samples must be kept.

Good storage conditions

  • Cool: heat speeds up seed ageing.
  • Dry: moisture causes moulds and loss of germination. Low humidity is best.
  • Dark and stable: avoid sunlight and big temperature changes.
  • Clean and pest-free: rodents and insects must not get in.
  • Secure: only authorised people may enter.

Many laboratories use a dedicated sample store or cold room with temperature and humidity monitoring. A simple store room can work if it is cool, dry and well managed.

Containers

Samples are kept in strong, sealed, labelled bags or containers. Moisture-proof containers protect seed from damp. Paper bags let seed breathe but can be damaged by rodents and damp.

lessons.title: Storing, finding and disposing of samples
lessons.html:
Storing, finding and disposing of samples

Putting samples into storage

  1. Check the sample is sealed and labelled with its laboratory number, crop, cultivar, lot number and date.
  2. Record the sample in the storage register or system with its location: room, shelf, box and position.
  3. Store samples in a logical order, for example by year and laboratory number, so they can be found quickly.
  4. Keep treated and untreated samples on separate, labelled shelves.
  5. Do not overload shelves or stack boxes so high that they fall.

Finding samples

When a sample is needed for a retest or complaint, find it using the register. Record when it was taken out, by whom and why. Return it to the same place, or record its new location.

Monitoring the store

  • Record temperature and humidity daily or as procedure says.
  • Check for signs of rodents and insects: droppings, chewed bags, live insects. Report them at once.
  • Keep the store clean; sweep up spilt seed.
  • Check doors, roofs and seals for leaks.

Disposing of old samples

When the storage period has ended, samples may be disposed of, but only with approval and according to procedure.

  • Check that the sample is not on hold for a complaint.
  • Record the disposal in the register: sample number, date, method and who approved.
  • Treated seed is hazardous. Dispose of it through the approved hazardous waste route. Never give it away or feed it to animals.
  • Untreated seed is disposed of as procedure says.

Safety

Wear gloves when handling treated samples. Use a step ladder for high shelves. Lift boxes correctly.

Key points

  • Stored samples are evidence for complaints and retests.
  • Store cool, dry, dark, clean and secure.
  • Record every sample's location and every removal.
  • Monitor temperature, humidity and pests.
  • Dispose only after the storage period, with approval; treated seed is hazardous waste.
